articles.title_zh: China and Southeast Asia pledge to avoid disputes during talks on South China Sea pact

MANILA, Philippines (AP) â China and Southeast Asian leaders will commit to avoid actions that can escalate disputes in the South China Sea in annual talks in the Philippine capital on Monday, aiming to foster a conducive atmosphere for negotiations on a non-aggression pact in the contested waters.
The territorial conflicts are high on the agenda in the summit meeting between leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Chinaâs premier, Li Qiang.
China, Taiwan and four ASEAN states â Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam â have been involved in the decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, a key global trade route. Confrontations have particularly escalated in recent years between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
Li expressed hope for the early conclusion of a âcode of conduct,â which can help foster peace and stability in the South China Sea, according to Chinaâs Xinhua news agency.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds ASEANâs rotational chairmanship, praised the progress made so far in the negotiations this year for the regional agreement.
The sides did not immediately issue a joint statement with more details of the talks. But a draft of the statement seen by The Associated Press has the Chinese and ASEAN leaders pledging âto exercise self-restraint in the conduct of activities that would complicate or escalate disputes and affect peace and stabilityâ in the disputed waters.
They will welcome the âpositive momentum and significant progressâ which have been achieved so far in the negotiations and âemphasize the need to maintain and promote an environment conducive to the negotiations,â according to the statement.
There had been an agreement to conclude the negotiations this year after more than 21 years of talks and consultations. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said on Sunday that both sides have agreed on about 80% of the total number of paragraphs, but three contentious issues remain unresolved and negotiations will continue next year when Singapore takes over ASEANâs leadership.
The last major sticking points are the geographic scope to be covered by the agreement, the definition of sensitive terms and whether the accord should be legally binding or not, according to Southeast Asian diplomats.
The South China Sea conflicts are a flashpoint in Asia which many fear could draw in the United States if a major conflict erupts. The U.S. lays no claims in the waters but has warned that itâs obligated to defend the Philippines, a longtime treaty ally in Asia, if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.title_zh: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.
But now fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report. The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
The Trump administration issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres on Monday, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models ahead of Trump's meeting with China President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. , external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump said Monday that he would welcome the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia - days after the chipmaker's co-founder was forced out over an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman - and insisted that no one had proven the woman was a spy.
"There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Trump told reporters as he left the White House to travel to Asia ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
“I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen. They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea. I recommended Tim Cook, who, as you know, built Apple, I recommended Tim Cook to go and do a job,” Trump continued.
Huang resigned last week after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a businesswoman that U.S. officials have described as a suspected asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined she had been recruited by the spy agency and tasked with influencing Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
In the days since, allies of the former Nvidia boss have been attempting to rally support for his return with an online petition that has thus far garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia shareholders and employees.
Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the founder and chief executive of the video game publisher Epic Games , were among major industry figures supporting an open letter calling for his return.
But Nvidia sources told CNBC on Monday that the company’s board is not considering bringing him back and is instead focused on a probe into whether his actions harmed American national security.
Pressed repeatedly on whether he accepted the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang, Trump questioned it.
"I don't know that she's a spy at all. Nobody's proven that," he said. "He probably shouldn't have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy."
Trump earlier offered a broader version of the same claim. "Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Asked whether he trusted the U.S. intelligence that the woman was a Chinese agent, and whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him so, Trump said he had not heard it.
"Who told me that? ... I haven't heard that. I haven't heard that," he said. "No, I don't know that she is a spy."
The president’s claims do not square exactly with what is publicly known about U.S. officials’ concerns over the affair.
According to The New York Times, Rubio was so alarmed by what intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum on her alleged recruitment and briefed Trump on it aboard Air Force One in May, en route to China.
But Trump brushed aside warnings from Rubio and nonetheless pressed ahead with a relationship that saw Huang become a frequent White House visitor after donating $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
The president defended the decision to keep selling chips to China and brushed aside the suggestion that his closeness to Huang had endangered national security. "It was not put at risk," he said Monday, before pivoting to a claim that the country "is now stronger than ever before."
Trump also dismissed statements from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC last week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted putting Megaspeed - a China-linked company run by Alice Huang and thought to be a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls - on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked about that, Trump said Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because ... you could have a blowup with China."
"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Different views," Trump said, declining to say whether he would replace Lutnick, who is traveling with him to China aboard Air Force One despite the scandal surrounding him and is scheduled to testify on the Nvidia affair before Congress in the next few weeks.
Huang was barred from selling Nvidia's most advanced processors, including its Blackwell line, to China, a restriction Trump defended while playing down its stakes.
"The only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics," Trump said. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing."
The president said he might raise the alleged spying operation with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet on Thursday but would not commit to doing so when pressed by reporters.
"I'll ask him what I want to ask him," he said.

articles.title_orig: Trump Admin Moves to Strangle China’s Remote Access to American AI Chips
articles.title_zh: Trump Admin Moves to Strangle China’s Remote Access to American AI Chips
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company.
Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."
In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. BIS said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
The interim rule notes that advances in cloud computing have made it easier for foreign nations to access American AI computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.
The Commerce Department wants to "ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests," the rule states.
The rule aims to align remote-access protections with existing controls governing physical access to sensitive American technology, the Commerce Department said.
Existing regulations on chip exports apply only to the most advanced semiconductors. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," President Trump said in remarks at the White House on Monday.
Mr. Trump is heading to Asia on Monday, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Chinese officials have said the country was not involved in Huang's affair with the suspected spy.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s stake in Nvidia grew to as much as $62 million before scandal broke out
articles.title_zh: Trump’s stake in Nvidia grew to as much as $62 million before scandal broke out
articles.content_orig:
The Washington Post says the stake is well above the $615,000 to $1.3 million Trump reported at the end of 2024
President Donald Trump outside the White House. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump owned Nvidia $NVDA shares worth somewhere from $13 million to $62 million at the close of August, according to an analysis of his financial disclosures by The Washington Post .
The disclosures leave out the most recent two months of trading because filings run behind, according to The Washington Post. The paper's range far exceeds the Nvidia holdings of between $615,000 and $1.3 million that Trump disclosed as of the end of 2024.
Trump's annual disclosure for 2025, which the Office of Government Ethics received on June 29, lists Nvidia stock valued at $1,000,001 to $5,000,000 in one investment account. The form shows $2,501 to $5,000 in capital gains income from the holding.
Reuters had not verified The Washington Post’s findings, and the White House and Nvidia had not responded to its requests for comment.
In December, Trump said the U.S. would permit Nvidia to sell China its H200 chips, the company's second-most-advanced AI processors, with a 25% cut of those sales going to the government, according to Reuters. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also declined to impose curbs on a firm suspected of redirecting Nvidia chips into China, according to The Washington Post.
The Washington Post also said Jensen Huang, who has since left his post as Nvidia 's chief, flew aboard Air Force One with Trump when the president last visited China.
The administration began permitting certain H200 shipments to China in January , with each application reviewed individually. That policy left in place separate restrictions covering organizations on the Commerce Department's Entity List. Nvidia 's board has also opened an independent probe into whether a foreign intelligence operation singled out Jensen Huang.
Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia , stepped down as CEO last week after controversy erupted over his involvement with Alice Huang, a businesswoman from China, according to Reuters. U.S. authorities suspect Alice Huang of intelligence ties to Beijing.
Jensen Huang ranks among the president's nearest allies in the tech industry's California hub, and their ties go back to at least 2025, according to Reuters. A Reuters reporter noticed Jensen Huang's name pop up on the screen of Trump's phone while the president was on a December call.
Nvidia is scheduled to release its fiscal third-quarter results on Tuesday, Nov. 17, according to Reuters.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.title_zh: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.content_orig:
Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. articles.title_orig: Stocks Fall Before Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Fall Before Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders reacted to more developments surrounding Nvidia .
The Nasdaq Composite declined 2.2%, while the S&P 500 fell 1.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 530 points, or 1%.
Shares of Nvidia were down more than 4%. The pressure came as a source familiar with the matter told CNBC that the chipmaker's board of directors is not discussing bringing back Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
Adding to the pressure, the Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent Nvidia's computing power located in other countries. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend also called for a " dramatic shakeup " at the company, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
The embattled chipmaker is preparing to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"Strong results won't resolve the questions surrounding Jensen's departure," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations. Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology and Intel lost 6%, while Advanced Micro Devices declined 5%. Memory chip name Sandisk pulled back about 7%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined 6%, while software stock Oracle moved down 4%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering . The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on a investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, the person said. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or Nvidia secrets.
Read the full story here .
— Seema Mody and Kif Leswing
Northcoast Research downgraded Costco Wholesale to neutral from buy on Monday after the stock's run higher this year.
The wholesale club has shown "remarkable success" as inflation drove shoppers into its stores, analyst Chuck Cerankosky said. However, shares currently trade at 48.4 times earnings.
"At multiples comparable to those of tech stocks and the rate at which the company is growing earnings, we believe shares of Costco Wholesale are valued fairly," he wrote in a note to clients.
The stock, which has gained 29% year to date, hit a 52-week high on Monday.
Despite uncertainty about the future of chipmaker Nvidia's leadership, there's strength ahead for semiconductors, according to Trivariate Research.
The firm expects "strong" earnings results from Nvidia this week and from memory maker Micron next month, supporting positive trends in returns over the next year.
"We think Semiconductors have a reasonable chance of being 50% higher in a year," Adam Parker at Trivariate wrote in a Sunday analysis.
Shares of Nvidia bounced on Thursday but failed to build on that progress on Friday, leading analysts at Wolfe to reconsider the $150 support level maintained last week.
"The stock successfully held that key $150 support level, after Thursday's notable intraday reversal. Unfortunately, the stock failed to build off of that reversal on Friday. Should price end up losing it, the next major support level sits around $100," Rob Ginsberg at Wolfe wrote in a Sunday note.
Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.
The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.
Read the full story here .
The three major averages kicked off the first trading session of the week in the red.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 declined 0.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 78 points, or 0.2%.
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China .
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." Read more .
Factory activity eased in  New York State during November though employment expanded at the fastest pace in more than four years, the regional Federal Reserve reported Monday.
The New York Fed's Empire State Manufacturing Index posted a reading of 7.8, down 18 points from October and below the Dow Jones consensus for 16.7. The index measures the difference between companies reporting growth against contraction, so a positive number still represents expansion.
Much of the decline came in new orders, which fell 20.2 points to 3.0. However, the employment index jumped to 18.1, growth of 7.8 points and its highest since June 2022. Prices also continued to climb but at a slower pace as the prices paid index fell 14 points to 45.9.
Nvidia continues to lose its luster, with two more Wall Street analysts lowering their price targets on the stock following a scandal that led to Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO.
Mizuho, which has an outperform on the chipmaker, lowered its price target on shares to $220 from $250. That still suggests 35% upside from Friday's close. UBS has a buy rating on the stock. It revised its price target on shares down to $240 from $300, which is 47% above the level at which Nvidia last closed.
"We believe ex-CEO Jensen was viewed as the global dealmaker 'AI banker', and key innovator," Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh said in a note to clients. "The significant NVDA ~32% stock decline from the Oct peak (vs. the SOX down 23%), reflects the 'Jensen/founder' premium lost. We believe the CEO departure also adds a 6-7-month management overhang, as [the] company comes under the US gov't microscope."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Check out CNBC's live blog here for more on the stocks making premarket moves.
— Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert
UniCredit 's takeover of Commerzbank has been given the go-ahead by European competition regulators.
The European Commission on Monday gave antitrust approval to the Italian lender's bid to take control of its German peer, following similar consent from the European Central Bank last month.
That now clears the path for the takeover, with UniCredit's integration plan expected to begin early next year.
"Our approval of UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank shows that it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's first executive vice-president for a clean, just and competitive transition.
Shares in Milan-listed UniCredit were 0.62% lower in morning trade. Commerzbank was down 1% in Frankfurt.

articles.title_orig: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.title_zh: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.content_orig:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — In early November, Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary-general tracked more than 100 Chinese military-linked vessels near his island.
But given its scale, the massive flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
They say China has sent an outsized number of its far-seas naval deployments to near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political dispute that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Takaichi told a Japanese House of Representatives committee session that month that a Chinese naval blockade or armed conflict involving Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for her own country not far away. China claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own and has not ruled out the use of force to take it.
“There is a direct link between Takaichi’s statement and the quality and quantity of deployments,” said Stephen Nagy, a visiting fellow with the Japan Institute for International Affairs think tank in Tokyo. “(China) is also sending a signal to Tokyo that if it continues its current position vis-a-vis Taiwan that Beijing will continue these activities.”
China is using the deployments, including live-fire drills, uncrewed drone missions and voyages by entire aircraft carrier groups, to exert an unrelenting, long-term pressure on Japan without violating international maritime laws, analysts said.
“By repeatedly transiting waters around the (southwestern) Islands, China is gradually normalizing PLA Navy activity within the first island chain, expanding its operational experience and creating a pattern of accepted presence,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence program.
The first island chain includes Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
“In other words, it is establishing facts on the ground, or rather at sea, that broaden its future freedom of action,” Yamamoto said.
In the seven weeks after Takaichi’s comment, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies logged a spike in “notable” PLA escalatory moves. Over 2025 overall, it said, China showed just a “slight increase” in the number of PLA naval vessels reported operating in waters around Japan, including an increase in the number of Chinese ships within the contiguous zone of the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China calls the Diaoyu.
Deployments near the uninhabited, Japanese-controlled Senkakus have “remained at very high levels” over the past year as before, while joint Sino-Russian missions around Japan and Chinese naval activity near the outlying Japanese islets around the Miyako Island “seem to have increased”, said Jeffrey Kingston, a professor specializing in Asian studies and history at Temple University, Japan Campus.
Chinese and Russian aircraft patrolled in June over the Sea of Japan, followed by a joint naval passage in July in the Miyako Strait near outlying Japanese islets. Chinese and Russian surveillance aircraft did five separate flights near Japan in October.
Spokespeople for the Chinese ministries of foreign affairs and national defense have called China’s military actions fair, valid and peaceful.
China is probably using military moves as one in a series of measures – some economic – to get back at Takaichi for her November 2025 remarks, Kingston said. “They haven’t forgotten, that’s for sure,” he said. “They are in various ways trying to put the screws on her.”
Officials in Beijing still want a retraction of the prime minister’s November 2025 comments but it’s unlikely, Kingston believes.
The Japanese government has verbally protested against Chinese military moves, tracked Chinese ships with its own, and scrambled fighter jets.
Tokyo is now considering a 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen (as high as $508 billion) defense spending plan for the five-year period beginning in April 2027, up from 43 trillion yen in the previous half-decade span, Japanese media outlets have reported.
“As the security environment becomes increasingly severe, cooperation with the ally and like-minded countries is indispensable to peace and stability in the region,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense said in an Oct. 29 statement after a meeting with defense officials from Australia, the Philippines and the United States.
The ministry, it said, “will continue to take advantage of various opportunities to further strengthen such cooperation.”

articles.title_orig: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.title_zh: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
Click here to download the JINSA Insight
At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19, President Donald Trump expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the summit’s sidelines to discuss getting their assistance in ending the war in Iran, while their two countries are helping sustain Tehran’s war effort. Yet, while the Trump administration has intensified military and economic pressure on Iran, it has simultaneously granted sanctions relief to Russia and refrained from targeting major Chinese financial institutions facilitating Iran’s illicit oil trade.
This contradictory approach risks leaving intact the foreign networks that could finance and rebuild Iran’s postwar rearmament in the event of an accord, as Chinese supplies helped Iran rebuild after the June 2025 12-Day War. Washington must confront the countries enabling Iran’s military recovery, and Shenzhen offers the perfect setting to do so.
Pressure on Iran, Relief for Its Backers
Since the United States and Israel launched Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion against Iran on February 28, the Trump administration has executed successive campaigns against Tehran’s revenue streams, procurement networks, and smuggling routes. The U.S. naval blockade, first implemented on April 13 and reimposed on July 14, has prevented, according to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Iran from earning more than $25 billion in crude oil revenue. The Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Fury , launched in April, targeted the financing infrastructure providing the basis for Iran’s trade and shadow-banking networks. In August, Operation Economic Outcast , or Economic “D-Day,” extended pressure on Tehran’s foreign financial enablers through sanctions and warning of secondary sanctions measures. The most recent initiative, CENTCOM’s Task Force Iron Gate , coordinates efforts against illicit shipments and revenue flows across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, routes the regime has increasingly utilized because of the U.S. blockade.
Despite these initiatives to go after Iran, Washington has pursued competing policies toward the Islamic Republic’s two primary foreign backers. The administration first provided sanctions waivers on Russian seaborne oil in March, a waiver which it extended twice, allowing Moscow to continue earning revenue from sanctioned oil shipments until the relief ultimately expired in June. In October, the administration authorized temporary transactions for Russian diesel until April 2027 and waived multiple provisions included in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The White House justified the Graham Act waivers by saying enforcing the sanctions provisions “would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
Washington has equally shied away from imposing its most consequential financial penalties on China. While the Treasury has imposed sanctions on China’s independent “teapot” oil refineries, Hong Kong-based intermediaries , and procurement companies enabling Iranian trade, it has stopped short of targeting the broader Chinese financial networks that facilitate Iranian oil payments and move the proceeds into the international financial system. When Xi visited Trump in September at the White House, the two extended their trade truce but reached no agreement on Chinese support for Tehran. The administration appears, therefore, reluctant to make any move jeopardizing U.S.-China economic relations even as it attempts to sever Iran’s foreign financial lifelines.
Russia’s Role in Arming Iran
Russia serves as one of Iran’s most consequential military and intelligence suppliers, helping Tehran lead operations against U.S. forces and regional partners. Since March, Moscow has, according to open-source reporting, provided upgraded Geran-2 attack drones , explosives , satellite imagery , and targeting intelligence that bolstered Iranian capabilities during the war. Reports also indicate that Russia is assisting Iran in developing advanced cruise missiles , which would strengthen Tehran’s ability to penetrate regional air defenses. Russia is equally aiding Iran’s strategy of using its proxy network to open a two-front war, as Moscow is reportedly sharing intelligence with the Houthis to carry out attacks on Red Sea shipping.
Russia’s assistance could become even more consequential after a cessation of hostilities. According to The Telegraph , Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered a November 5 letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei requesting Russian S-400 air defense systems. Tehran has also pursued Russia’s 4.5-generation Su-35 fighters and will reportedly receive them following the war’s conclusion . A prewar Iranian parliamentary memorandum also obtained by The Telegraph outlined plans to deepen cooperation with Moscow on missiles, drones, and air defenses, suggesting that Tehran views foreign military assistance, especially that from Russia, as a central pillar of its long-term survival. Of course, Russia’s war in Ukraine limits what weaponry it can spare to its Iranian partner, but even selective transfers of air defense components and drone technology would raise the cost of future U.S. or Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear and missile facilities.
China’s Role in Financing Iran’s Recovery
China has been more cautious than Russia about transferring complete weapons systems during the ongoing war, but it has played perhaps the largest role in financing Iran’s reconstruction through oil purchases and providing critical components for weapons systems to operate. According to prewar statistics, Beijing bought about 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports through independent teapot refineries, making it responsible for an estimated 45 percent of Iran’s total government budget. Iran’s reliance on China has continued during the war, with Kpler data identifying Beijing as the only purchaser of Iranian crude in October. On the weapons front, Chinese firms have supplied Iran with the crucial missile propellant precursor sodium perchlorate , as well as dual-use drone components . The full extent of direct Chinese military assistance during the current war remains uncertain, but the presence of these procurement networks could again accelerate Tehran’s rearmament should hostilities end.
Iran is reportedly constructing more durable infrastructure in China aimed at circumventing U.S. sanctions. According to a recent Iran International report , citing a leaked letter from Iran’s Oil Ministry, Iran now controls a terminal in the Ningbo-Zhoushan free trade zone, holds stakes in docks in Shandong province, and owns seven storage tanks in Dalian, Huizhou, Dongying, Weifang, and Zhoushan. This infrastructure allows tankers in the fleet of Hossein Shamkhani, son of the late Khamenei adviser Ali Shamkhani, 51 of whose vessels the Treasury has sanctioned, to unload near refinery pipelines and allows Iran to store its crude in China before securing buyers, which mitigates the impact of existing Treasury designations and suggests that Iran is building sanctions-resistant oil facilities in China with Beijing’s tacit approval or acquiescence.
The Precedent of the 12-Day War
Iran’s recovery in the wake of previous U.S. and Israeli air campaigns against it is a case in point as to why battlefield success alone cannot guarantee lasting strategic gains. Israel’s October 2024 strikes on Iran reportedly decreased Tehran’s capacity to produce solid fuel for ballistic missiles by approximately 93 percent, from enough for 14 missiles per week to just one. Eight months later, operations during the 12-Day War destroyed additional missile production facilities, launchers, and stockpiles, again reducing Iran’s operational arsenal. articles.title_orig: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.title_zh: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
articles.title_zh: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department announced Monday it is cracking down on a loophole that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
It marks the first government response since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his multitrillion-dollar chipmaker after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy — and as romances with at least two Nvidia employees surfaced.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third countries, according to a Monday press release .
It was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” according to the release.
It came after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized the Commerce Department for not acting sooner against Megaspeed — an Nvidia customer for whom Huang lover Alice Huang, no relation, worked –which has been accused of illegally diverting sensitive AI chips to China.
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump about the former Nvidia boss’ romance with Alice Huang last spring, according to reports. Last week, Jensen Huang resigned following bombshell revelations about that relationship and an affair with senior Nvidia exec Kimberly Powell.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s team for the Chinese spy mess, saying the Treasury, State Department, Defense Department and US Trade Representative had been trying “for months” to blacklist Megaspeed.
In a Sunday letter addressed to Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate commerce committee – urged the commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
“Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology.”
Asked about reports that Rubio had briefed Trump on the alleged Chinese spy plot targeting Huang, the president said Monday, “I haven’t heard that.”
“I don’t know that she [Alice Huang] is a spy,” the commander-in-chief told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”
Trump also said that the national security of the country “was not put at risk” and that he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO.
Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named as interim CEO , and the chipmaking giant has hired an outside firm to seek a permanent replacement.
With Huang, one of the driving forces of the AI boom, missing in action, investors have been panicking that Nvidia’s dealmaking could slow — a potentially massive monkey wrench for the sector after recent weeks have seen Wall Street get jittery about the tech trade.

articles.title_orig: Cantwell calls out U.S. Secretary of Commerce for allowing China access to advanced AI technology
articles.title_zh: Cantwell calls out U.S. Secretary of Commerce for allowing China access to advanced AI technology
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: 7 Things We Just Learned About the Next-Gen Xbox
articles.title_zh: 7 Things We Just Learned About the Next-Gen Xbox
articles.content_orig:
As part of Xbox's 25th anniversary celebrations today, we've been treated to a new digital version of a magazine that was given out at Seattle FanFest earlier this week, available to read in full over on the official Xbox Wire website .
The bit that's getting most attention concerns Xbox Project Helix - the new next-gen console that's currently in the works over at Xbox HQ. The brand's VP of Next Generation, Jason Ronald, shares tons of new information across four pages in the magazine, helping to give us a better idea of what to expect from the upcoming console.
There's one section in particular that's getting all the interest on social media right now, where he clarifies that Project Helix is definitely a console that can play PC games, and definitely not a PC that happens to play console games.
"We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
Beyond this, Ronald talks in depth about loads of other aspects of what they're aiming for with Project Helix, and as mentioned, there's so much detail that it spreads across four pages of the magazine.
In the interest of highlighting as much as possible though, we thought we'd transcribe all of most notable quotes from the magazine down below, whereas you can read the added context inside of the magazine article itself.
Here are more of the key bits from the magazine article:
"When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine - one that removes all barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games."
"We don't think the next generation is defined by 8K or 240 hertz, or some of the traditional metrics - it's really about gameplay innovation. It's about deeper immersion. It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering, to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering."
"When I think about what makes a console magical, it's that it just makes my games instantly accessible and ready to play in an instant. I don't have to worry about updating my operating system, updating drivers, configuring different settings - things like that. The hardware and the experience is entirely designed around playing games."
"The very first next-generation conversations we had were with all of our first-party studios. That was absolutely foundational to the design of what we've done with Project Helix - talking about where they saw the future of game design going, where they saw the future of their franchises going, and what was constraining their creative ambition."
"With Xbox One, I think we got so focused on expanding our aperture that we lost sight of what truly is magical, which is players, developers, and the games that they love. We have to build the best platform for game developers to deliver their creative vision."
"The other thing, and I think this is something that is unique about Xbox, is we have to be connected to the community. A lot of the features that people have come to love and expect from Xbox have actually been driven directly by community feedback. I think that's really core to the soul of who Xbox is, because if you're in touch with your player base, you never go wrong if you focus on what their needs are."
"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and a platform designer, it's also one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable."
"This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years."
"The ROG Xbox Ally was really an opportunity for us to learn alongside our player base with a lot of these concepts and the ideas that we had: being able to play libraries from across multiple different storefronts, understanding how PC games and console games can show up together in a unified library. The feedback that we've gotten from players has fundamentally informed and altered our plans of how it actually shows up in a future console. Players shared where we met the mark and areas we needed to improve or approach differently. So absolutely, we view the Ally as a precursor to what we're doing with Helix - but it's informed by a lot of the design concepts we have for Helix."
Sorry for the wall of quotes, but we thought you might find all of this pretty interesting! It's not even the full extent of what Ronald had to say, as he also touched on the importance of game preservation to the Xbox platform in general, as well as how Project Helix will seemingly have a bespoke UI, but one that still feels familiar to Xbox fans.
Of course, we're still waiting on concrete details about what Helix will look like, how much it'll cost, how significant the PC integration will be, and loads of other things that will give us a much better picture of how it'll shape up.
It seems like we won't be getting that this year though, and if rumours are to be believed, Xbox might even be releasing a first-party handheld in 2027 before the Project Helix console in 2028 . Who knows... plans can always change.
For now, let us know what you think about this latest info on Xbox Project Helix down below, and we definitely recommend reading the full Xbox 25th anniversary magazine for yourself - we wish we could buy one to be honest!

articles.title_orig: Someone rebuilt old Android versions in your browser, and it's an instant nostalgia hit [Gallery]
articles.title_zh: Someone rebuilt old Android versions in your browser, and it's an instant nostalgia hit [Gallery]
articles.content_orig:
The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia.
Built on the back of AOSP builds for classic Nexus devices, “Android Time Machine” lets you quickly  access older Android versions. Specifically, Android 2.1 Eclair through Android 7.1.2 Nougat.
The simulator runs within the shell of a matching Nexus smartphone on a desktop browser, or to fit your actual smartphone if you run it on Android.
Versions and simulated smartphones include :
The best part here is how it works on your actual smartphone. When launched in fullscreen, it  scales to match your phone’s screen – meaning it fits even devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s smaller outer display (it just shows the desktop version when open).
Since this is running through the browser and not an actual Android build, you won’t get a perfect replication. Performance is a little hit or miss, especially with certain animations, but it works really well overall.
The browser even simulates results from each era (oh, to go back to when Google Search wasn’t an absolute mess ). Similarly, Google apps and the camera are filled with placeholders since the web app can’t access the actual camera or connect to the internet to sign into a Google account.
Seeing things like the boot animations and live wallpapers from classic Nexus phones, as well as peeking back at lost apps like Google+ and Play Music, is just such a fun little piece of nostalgia.
“Android Time Machine” is free, and the source code is available on GitHub .

articles.title_orig: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
articles.title_zh: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
articles.content_orig:
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

articles.title_orig: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches
articles.title_zh: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches
articles.content_orig:
WARSAW, POLAND—Excavations within the medieval Great Church of Jesus in northern Sudan’s Old Dongola uncovered a section of the original cathedral floor for the first time, according to an IFL Science report. Old Dongola was the capital of Makuria, a flourishing Nubian kingdom that converted to Christianity in the sixth century A.D. The cathedral once dominated the ancient metropolis, measuring 154 feet wide and 187 long, and standing over six stories high. It was one of the most monumental and important Christian buildings in Nubia, likely serving as the seat of the Bishop of Dongola, one of the most senior Christian figures in medieval sub-Saharan Africa. The recent work was a joint endeavor conducted by Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology at the University of Warsaw and Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums. In addition to the original floor where medieval worshippers once walked, the team unearthed the base of a vast staircase. “In the history of architecture, certain buildings emerge that, to use a modern term, become trendsetters. Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, modern-day Istanbul, is certainly one such example,” said Artur Obłuski, expedition director from the University of Warsaw. “The Great Church of Jesus appears to be a natural candidate for such a role in Nubia, and perhaps even in this part of Africa.” To read about other finds from Old Dongola, go to “ A Painted Prayer ,” one of A RCHAEOLOGY ’s Top 10 Discoveries of 2023.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia set to deliver first life-after-Huang briefing
articles.title_zh: Nvidia set to deliver first life-after-Huang briefing
articles.content_orig:
The credit markets were already choking on AI-related debt issuance and now we have the Nvidia surprise. Let’s see what to expect now.
You've reached your free article limit
You've read 0 of 1 free Pro articles.
The buy-the-dip urge remains strong in this market. That was demonstrated again last week as the Nasdaq rose 2.5%, a week after the tech-heavy index tumbled 3.4%. The rally happened even as the CEO of Nvidia Corp. ( NVDA ) was forced out. Nvidia has since given back some $1.6 trillion of market value from its highs. And this saga may not be over as a couple of big investors and Elon Musk have publicly come out and stated the board of the giant chipmaker should consider reinstating Jensen Huang.
Their support is not that surprising, given Nvidia operates as a “banker” throughout the AI ecosystem. It takes equity stakes in firms such as in neocloud providers CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius N.V. ( NBIS ). The company also acts like a financial backstop for huge AI data center projects, such as the $500 billion effort planned for Ohio. How the recent midterm results in that state will impact that endeavor, however, is an unknown.
In addition, the company has been a huge advocate for open-source models. And to be fair, Mr. Huang’s ouster at Nvidia does feel somewhat orchestrated. Much like the surge of stories around how dangerous AI could become around Labor Day that resulted in congressional hearings. The timing is also curious given the coming Anthropic PBC ( ANT ) IPO, and the open-source models are an existential threat to frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI.
The push for more federal regulation would be beneficial to these companies if it created a duopoly and would provide a considerable moat for a sector that currently doesn’t have much of one. The commerce secretary’s job seems hanging by a thread and it is unknown if Nvidia empowered shell companies to evade sanctions on AI chips going to China. In summary, it feels like this tale is just getting started, so get your popcorn ready as this story may have more twists and turns than a novella.
The other big theme last week was around inflation and interest rates. The October consumer price index reading came in hotter than expected. The October producer price index report came in a bit cooler than the consensus. That said, the 12-month rise was the highest since November 2022. Not surprisingly, interest rates shot up. It didn’t help that the federal government sold over $750 billion in new Treasury securities last week. After touching 4.82% on Nov. 5, the yield on the 10-Year Treasury closed the week near 5.15%. The 30-year treasury yield ended the week just under 5.5%.
With the two-year Treasury yield significantly above the Fed Funds rate, the market is projecting a couple of additional rate hikes on the horizon. A quarter percentage point increase for the Fed Funds rate is all but certain at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting with a very slight probability of a half-point hike.
The credit markets were choking on AI-related debt issuance as it was. Last week’s news around Nvidia and a surge in rates raises considerable questions on how this buildout will be financed going forward. A significant slowdown in AI infrastructure capital spending growth feels almost certain in 2027 after an over 90% surge this year. This will have considerable negative impacts on economic growth and doesn’t feel like it priced into the market despite last week’s buyer’s enthusiasm.
At the time of publication, Jensen had no position in any security mentioned.
