articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock ended 2025 at $186.50. As I write this, shares trade near $166, about 11% lower this year with about six weeks of trading left. On Nov. 12, the day the company announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO, the stock briefly dropped to $148.80.
Unless shares get back to $186.50 or above by year-end, 2026 will be the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker's first losing calendar year since 2022. It'd be just the eighth losing year in the stock's history as a public company.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
For shareholders, the history is encouraging, because the growth stock gained the year after five of its seven earlier down years. But the big rebounds all followed far deeper losses than this year's, at times when Nvidia's profits were shrinking. Neither is true now.
The first group is the deep sell-offs. Nvidia stock dropped 83% in 2002, 76% in 2008, 31% in 2018 and 50% in 2022, and each time, profits were falling by year-end.
Nvidia's net income fell 49% in fiscal 2003 (the company's fiscal year ends in late January, so fiscal 2003 closely matches calendar 2002). Fiscal 2009 saw a $30 million net loss, after a profit of around $798 million a year earlier. And fiscal 2023's net income sank 55% to about $4.4 billion.
Notably, even 2018 fits. Fiscal 2019's profit climbed for the full year, but net income in the quarter ending in January 2019 fell 49% year over year.
Each of the four losing years was followed by a big rebound. The stock more than doubled in both 2003 and 2009, gained 76% in 2019 and more than tripled in 2023.
The second group looks very different. Nvidia stock dropped 18% in 2010, 10% in 2011, and 12% in 2012. Those were three mild losses in a row, and profits were mostly rising throughout.
Net income swung to $253 million in fiscal 2011 from the previous year's $68 million loss. It then grew 130% to $581 million in fiscal 2012 before dropping 3% in fiscal 2013.
And there was no quick rebound. It wasn't until 2013 that shares gained again, rising 31%.
On both counts, this year looks more like 2010 through 2012. An 11% decline is mild by Nvidia's standards. And profits aren't falling -- they're climbing fast.
Showing how far the business has come, Nvidia's net income grew 65% in fiscal 2026 (which ended in January) to around $120 billion. In the first half of fiscal 2027, the company earned $118 billion, almost matching all of the last fiscal year. Second-quarter net income alone rose 126% year over year to $59.7 billion.
And operating income, which strips out Nvidia's gains on its investments, climbed 19% from the first quarter to the second.
I think that difference matters for a shareholder. The big rebounds came after the stock had already priced in shrinking profits, so a recovery in earnings had a lot of room to lift the price. This year, shares dipped while profits kept climbing. That arguably makes a 2023-style surge less likely in 2027.
Even so, it also leaves the stock cheaper relative to what the company earns. Based on analysts' average estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year ending in January 2028), Nvidia trades at around 11 times earnings as I write. FactSet put the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500 at about 18 on Nov. 5. Put another way, every dollar of Nvidia's expected profit costs investors less than the typical large company's.
Of course, where the stock heads next depends much more on Nvidia's earnings than on the calendar. The fiscal third-quarter report is due Tuesday, Nov. 17, and management's outlook for the fiscal fourth quarter could indicate whether profits can keep climbing at that first-half pace.
A mild losing year can also become a run of them, as it did from 2010 to 2012. But even that stretch was followed by a stock that gained in each of the next five years.
What does a down 2026 mean, then, for somebody who holds Nvidia shares going into 2027? On its own, not much. Going by 2010 to 2012, I wouldn't count on a quick rebound after a mild drop like this. But with profits still climbing and shares at around 11 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, I wouldn't sell the stock over a losing year.

articles.title_orig: Trump Says He’s Open to Reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia Chief
articles.title_zh: Trump Says He’s Open to Reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia Chief
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said on Monday that he was open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the head of Nvidia, his latest public expression of support for the tech executive who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.
“I would not mind; I would not mind that,” Mr. Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House as he departed for a trip to Asia, including a stop in China.
“I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another,” he added.
The president cast doubt on whether Alice Huang , the woman with whom Mr. Huang had a relationship, was actually a spy.
“I don’t know that she is a spy,” Mr. Trump said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

articles.title_orig: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Lumentum, Sandisk, Coinbase, Nvidia & more
articles.title_zh: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Lumentum, Sandisk, Coinbase, Nvidia & more
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence trade dropped to start the week, as "picks and shovels" plays declined alongside Nvidia.
Lumentum, Sandisk and Bloom Energy tumbled alongside the chip giant ahead of Nvidia's earnings due Tuesday afternoon. Coinbase and Strategy, both of which are tied to bitcoin, also dropped as traders went risk-off.
Investors sought shelter in consumer staples, lifting the Consumer Staples Select SPDR ETF (XLP) to a record high.
Procter & Gamble, the maker of Tide laundry detergent and Pampers baby diapers, as well as Church & Dwight, the company behind OxiClean, touched 52-week highs.
Follow along as CNBC highlights the biggest stock market moves of the day.
Shares of Nvidia touched session lows after CNBC reported, citing a source familiar, that the chip company's board of directors isn't considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO.
The stock was last down about 3.7% on the day.
Read more from CNBC on this latest Nvidia development here .
Strategy dropped 7% and Coinbase Global fell 6% as equities tied to cryptocurrencies weakened alongside bitcoin , which briefly fell to $62,000 over the weekend before recovering Monday. Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August since Friday as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated as market liquidity weakened and risk appetite dropped off.
Bitcoin is coming off its sixth straight weekly decline .
— Scott Schnipper, Tanaya Macheel
"Picks and shovels" stocks tied to the AI data center build-out effort resumed their tumble on Monday.
Photonics stock Lumentum dropped more than 7%, as did memory maker Sandisk . Chipmaker Intel and data center power stock Bloom Energy declined more than 6%.
The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was heading for its third consecutive losing day, down 4% Monday afternoon.
The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLP) ticked higher to reach an all-time high as traders dropped tech for safer corners of the stock market.
Staples and healthcare were the only positive sectors of the S&P 500 as of noon Monday, with the XLP up about 0.2% on the day.
Manufacturers of household products Procter & Gamble , Church & Dwight and Colgate-Palmolive all advanced more than 1% to hit 52-week highs. Big-box store chain Costco Wholesale also inched up to a 52-week high, last trading up less than 1%.
Shares of Tyson Foods advanced more than 9% on better-than-expected quarterly results.
The company delivered earnings per share of 61 cents on revenue of $14.59 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet expected a profit of 53 cents per share on revenue of $14.1 billion. Tyson is known for its portfolio of food products which include beef, pork, chicken, and prepared foods.
To be sure, the company's guidance for fiscal 2027 was cause for some pause. Management expects operating income of $1.7 billion to $2.15 billion, which is in line with FactSet's $2.13 billion estimate.
The company also expects beef production to decrease by about 2% next year and anticipates an operating income loss in the segment.
L3Harris , a defense electronics contractor, fell 4% after the Trump administration blamed it for Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide groundstop of all airline traffic.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday said the ground stop occurred while L3Harris was performing routine maintenance. "This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment," Duffy said at a press conference.
Cancelation rates for the top six U.S. airlines reached 32% Friday and 30% on Saturday, according to  FlightAware data analyzed by UBS.
Shares for Johnson & Johnson gained 1.4% after the company announced it will acquire clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion.
Johnson & Johnson also announced it will receive $750 million from Blackstone Life Sciences to fully cover the Phase 3 development of OLN324, an "investigational, next-generation bispecific antibody."
Shares for Aramark fell more than 5% after the company posted fiscal fourth-quarter results that missed the expectations.
The operator of cafeterias, hospital kitchens and sports stadium food stands reported adjusted earnings per share of 71 cents on revenue of $5.29 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet expected a profit of 75 cents per share on revenue of $5.03 billion.
The company also expects adjusted earnings per share to increase between 20% and 25% and revenue to grow between 9% and 10% for the full year.
Shares related to airlines, including American Airlines , Delta and United Airlines were down over 1% after  the Federal Aviation Administration briefly issued a nationwide ground stop on all flights on Friday, causing flight delays and travel disruptions. On Sunday, President Donald Trump blamed the Biden administration for the FAA stop.
"The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad," he wrote on social media.
Shares of Stagwell popped over 1% after StoneX upgraded the digital-first marketing company to buy from hold.
"Our Boston-hosted NDR last wk with CEO Mark Penn left us more optimistic on Enterprise tech solutions top line and incremental margin prospects," wrote analyst Alex Lavigne.
Lavigne added while its concerned Stagwell is losing small and midsize business customers, he has a positive outlook that its growing technology and other higher-margin businesses will be profitable and make up for those losses.
Lavigne set Stagwell's price target to $15, implying a 33% upside from Friday's close.
SpaceX gained slightly after its spacecraft was able to catch the upper stage portion of its Starship rocket from orbit . This comes after the first phase of the flight on Friday was unsuccessful, with SpaceX unable to catch and recover the rocket's booster and exploding before it fell into the Gulf of Mexico.
Yeti dropped 1.3% after Goldman Sachs downgraded the beverage container manufacturer to neutral from buy.
"While our checks ahead of the print pointed to a more measured backdrop, YETI's 3Q update revealed a more meaningful softening in US DTC growth momentum. In combination with our forecast for US wholesale to slow following wholesale replenishment, we now see a tougher sales backdrop ahead for the US business which we believe will limit multiple expansion for the stock," wrote analyst Brooke Roach.
Take-Two Interactive shares were up more than 3% ahead of Thursday's release of the much-anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI" video game. Jefferies over the weekend also reiterated its buy rating and $300 price target on Take-Two, saying "GTA VI is just the beginning."
"While the launch itself is well understood, we believe the bigger opportunity is the duration of the GTA VI monetization cycle. GTA Online and an eventual PC release could provide meaningful incremental bookings into FY28, neither of which we believe is embedded in FY27 guidance. We continue to model FY27 bookings above the high end of guidance and see upside to our $10 FY28 EPS estimate as the GTA VI ecosystem scales," wrote analyst James Heaney.
Nvidia shares were down 2.2%, adding to their steep losses from last week, as traders brace for the company's fiscal third-quarter results due Tuesday. Analysts at UBS and Mizuho trimmed their price targets on the chipmaker.

articles.title_orig: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs in Children as Young as 6
articles.title_zh: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs in Children as Young as 6
articles.content_orig:
Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.
When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.
"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.
In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.
While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.
In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.
But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.
"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.
Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.
Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.
"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

articles.title_orig: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update via leaker
articles.title_zh: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update via leaker
articles.content_orig:
Ten years ago, Apple skipped the iPhone 9 and used the iPhone X to end the wide forehead and chin that had defined the first decade of the iPhone. The notch was mocked. Face ID was doubted. The gesture interface was called a learning curve. In September 2017, Craig Federighi took the stage, held up a phone, and Face ID failed to unlock. He tried another unit. It failed again. The room laughed. Within hours, the internet was pasting the notch onto cats, moustaches, and cartoon faces.
A decade later, the notch is remembered as the starting point of the full-screen era.
The supply chain now points to a similar jump. Apple is expected to skip the iPhone 19 and release the iPhone 20 in 2027, the twentieth-anniversary model. The leaks describe four-sided curved glass, a front that hides as many holes as possible, a glass back, two sizes around 6.41 and 6.96 inches, under-display Face ID, solid-state buttons, eSIM-only designs, and a custom image sensor.
Will it be great? It can be great in one narrow sense. It probably will not be great in the way the iPhone X was. Its greatness will come from pushing the iPhone to the edge of “a single slab of glass” through optical tricks and structural compromise. It will mark the next decade of iPhone design. It will not be a flawless object.
Jony Ive’s old ambition was to turn the iPhone into “a single slab of glass.” The iPhone 20 leaks suggest Apple is finally moving toward that shape: a four-sided micro-curved glass cover, curved glass wrapping around the sides, and a front that reads as borderless.
It is not a pure glass body. A pure glass chassis failed for engineering reasons. Glass is hard but brittle. It handles compression well and edge flaws badly. The more complex the curve, the harder it is to control thickness, curvature, and residual stress. Joining multiple glass panels is worse. The adhesive must be strong, transparent, and durable. Increase bond strength and the seam becomes visible. Hide the seam and structural strength drops.
Apple’s solution keeps a metal frame. Curved glass extends toward the sides. A metal band carries the structure. To make that band strong enough, Apple is using 3D-printed titanium. Laser powder-bed printing builds internal lattice structures and micro-textures that CNC cutters cannot reach. The USB-C port housing on the iPhone Air already uses a 3D-printed titanium part. Under a 50-micron microscope, the surface shows a chain-like circular pattern. Those micro-textures help metal bite into glass or plastic, improving mechanical locking and water sealing.
The display itself is not bent. The OLED panel stays flat. The glass cover is thermally bent. Pixels do not reach the edge. The curved glass refracts light and hides the border. What you see as a borderless front is glass doing a refraction trick for your eye.
That is the first compromise. The “single slab of glass” is a visual effect built on a flat OLED panel, a curved cover, and a metal frame. It is a real design change. It is not a material revolution.
Under-display Face ID is moving forward. A full Face ID system needs a flood illuminator, a dot projector, and an infrared camera. The iPhone 18 Pro is expected to put the infrared camera under the OLED panel, shrinking the Dynamic Island for the first time. The next step is to put the dot projector under the display as well. Apple’s patents describe compact projector modules that combine the flood illuminator and dot projector, and planar optical waveguides that guide infrared light through the gaps between display pixels.
The under-display front camera is a different problem. The folding iPhone Duo is expected to be the first production iPhone with an in-display selfie camera on the inner screen. Early reports describe the image as gray and soft. The pixel layer blocks light and diffracts it. Android makers have spent years on the same problem. The common fix is to remove some subpixels above the lens and increase pixel spacing to raise transmittance. Display sharpness drops. Selfies stay hazy.
On a straight-slab flagship that relies on one screen, Apple will not gamble on the main selfie camera. The iPhone 20 will likely ship with an under-display Face ID system and a punch-hole front camera. The pill-shaped Dynamic Island shrinks to a single “Dynamic Hole.” That is progress. It is not the hole-less front people have been asking for.
The rest of the body loses holes. Solid-state buttons are back in testing. Apple prototyped solid-state volume and power buttons during the iPhone 15 Pro cycle under the code name “Project Bongo,” then paused. Patents continued. The twentieth-anniversary model is the obvious launch window. eSIM removes the SIM tray, especially in China as carrier activation flows improve. Screen-based audio can replace the top earpiece. The iPad mini already ships an “Acoustic Display” system. A woofer vibrates the display for low frequencies. Tweeters sit between the glass and the aluminum chassis. The iPhone does not have the same panel area, so the likely implementation is screen audio for the earpiece and a reduced bottom speaker grille.
The iPhone 20 will be the closest iPhone to a hole-less body. It will still have a hole.
The display is expected to move to tandem OLED, the structure Apple introduced on the M4 iPad Pro. Two OLED layers stacked together raise full-screen brightness without pushing single-layer emission harder. COE, color filters integrated into the OLED encapsulation to remove the polarizer, has been discussed for the iPhone. Supply-chain reports say mass production challenges have pushed COE on straight-slab iPhones to 2029. The iPhone 20 gets a brighter, thinner display. It does not get every advanced panel technology at once.
The camera is where the engineering becomes concrete. The iPhone 18 Pro is expected to introduce a physical variable aperture. Apple is moving beyond software-simulated depth of field and putting a mechanical iris into the lens module. The iPhone 20 is expected to keep it and add a 1/1.12-inch main sensor. The iPhone 14 Pro through the current models have used a 1/1.28-inch sensor. The larger sensor collects more light.
The bigger change is Apple’s custom LOFIC sensor. In a patent titled “Image Sensor With Stacked Pixels Having High Dynamic Range And Low Noise,” Apple describes a pixel design that replaces the traditional 4T circuit with a 3T design. It removes the transfer gate to make room for a LOFIC circuit. When the photodiode fills with charge, excess electrons do not spill into a white highlight. They flow laterally into two capacitors with different capacities. The sensor uses a stacked architecture. The top chip handles light capture and overflow charge. The bottom logic chip handles noise reduction and signal processing, with an internal current-storage circuit canceling dark noise from sensor heat.
If it ships, the result is a single exposure that holds highlight, midtone, and shadow detail. Dynamic range lands around 120 dB, close to 20 stops. MacRumors reports that Apple’s stacked sensor is physically more compact than Sony’s current offering. A 1/1.12-inch sensor with LOFIC and a variable aperture would force Apple to redesign the internal stack. The camera bump, the logic board, the thermal path, and the battery layout all change. The iPhone 20’s biggest internal job may be the rearrangement, not the sensor alone.
The chip is expected to be the A21 Pro on a 2nm process. That is a routine iteration. The shift is where the compute goes: more on-device AI, more image processing, more thermal management. The iPhone 18 Pro is already expected to enlarge the VC heat plate to three times the previous area and redesign the chip packaging to conduct heat more directly. That reduces the need to use an aluminum frame as a heat sink. It also makes a titanium frame easier to justify.

articles.title_zh: AMD, Broadcom stocks sink on tighter US chip rules, CoreWeave and Nebius shares drop
articles.content_orig:
Advanced Micro Devices (Nasdaq: AMD) was one of several chip stocks pulling back in response to a new rule announced this morning by the Commerce Department restricting chip exports to Southeast Asia.
The move comes in response to revelations that the Singaporean data center company Megaspeed had been funneling Nvidia chips to China against export rules.
As of 10:53 a.m. ET, AMD stock was down 4.4% in response to the announcement, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF was down 4%, showing the whole sector was getting hit.
Image source: Getty Images.
Like Nvidia, AMD had also taken a write-down on chips designed for export to China when stricter rules were applied early last year, so AMD might also have similar exposure to Southeast Asia.
AMD is the closest competitor to Nvidia in AI processors, and its chips like MI350X look set to face greater restrictions. In 2025, 12.4% of AMD's revenue came from sales to Singapore, which is one of the countries on the new list, meaning those sales could now be blocked or delayed.
NASDAQ · As of 12:42 PM ET 11/16/26
Investors have been trying to parse what the crisis at Nvidia means for AMD. Nvidia dominates the massive data-center GPU market, while AMD is a distant #2. Nvidia's challenges arguably create opportunity for AMD, but stricter oversight from the federal government is now a consequence, and investor enthusiasm, as well as Nvidia financial support for the broader AI ecosystem, are at risk as well.
AMD initially rose on the news that Huang was stepping down, but the stock has now given up those gains and then some. AMD investors will want to look out for any response in the stock when Nvidia reports earnings tomorrow, as that could be a signal of what to expect going forward.

articles.title_orig: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly
articles.title_zh: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly
articles.content_orig:
Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.
The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.
Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower.
On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday.
Bitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets.
On Friday, the dollar index — which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin — reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
"A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia's results add to the tech selling," he said. "The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over."
Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, said he's monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides.
"Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling," he said. "For a recovery to hold, spot buyers need to keep showing up after the forced selling has passed."

articles.title_orig: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.title_zh: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-four Shia Muslims, most of them clerics, have been sentenced to life in prison in Bahrain on Iran-linked terrorism charges, according to a UK-based human rights group.
The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said another five people were handed 15-year prison sentences by the High Criminal Court in Manama.
The advocate general confirmed the sentences but did not give the number of defendants or identify them. He said they were accused of establishing a terrorist group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
BIRD condemned the verdicts, saying there had been "credible allegations of torture, coerced confessions, and severe restrictions on the defence".
Authorities in the Sunni Muslim-ruled kingdom have reportedly detained hundreds of people, most of them members of its Shia majority, on suspicion of espionage and terrorism offences since the start of the US and Israel's war with regional Shia power Iran in February.
Dozens have also been stripped of their Bahraini citizenship after being accused by the government of "sympathy and praise for Iran's hostile and criminal acts".
Iran has launched thousands of missiles and drones at Bahrain and other Gulf Arab states hosting US forces during the war. On Sunday, the Bahraini military said it had intercepted "several Iranian aerial attacks".
Fifty-six of the defendants sentenced on Monday were arrested in May and June.
BIRD said 47 of them were Shia clerics - including Sheikh Mohammed Sanqour and Sheikh Ali al-Sadadi, who led Friday prayers at the Imam al-Sadiq Grand Mosque in Duraz, and Sayed Moosa al-Alwedaie, who served as imam at the Grand Mosque in Ras Rumman - and nine were their affiliates, including religious reciters.
The 13 other defendants - including the exiled cleric Sheikh Isa Qassim, who holds the religious rank of ayatollah and ​is widely regarded as the spiritual ​leader of Bahrain's Shia community - were tried in absentia, it said. Bahraini authorities said most of them were in Iran.
The 64 defendants faced charges including establishing a terrorist group, which the Public Prosecution said was linked to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), and calling for the suspension of the provisions of the constitution and a change in the system of government.
The prosecution alleged that they had incited terrorist acts and promoted "Velayat-e Faqih" (rule by the supreme jurist), which is the backbone of Iran's theocratic system.
The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants and imposed prison sentences ranging from 15 years to life, the advocate general and head of the Terrorist Crimes Prosecution announced . The court also fined some of the defendants $265,000 (£200,000) and ordered the confiscation of $21.2m (£16m) for charitable purposes.
The director of BIRD, Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, said the verdicts were "deeply unjust" and constituted "an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain's Shia community".
Reuters news agency cited a person close to the clerics' defence teams as describing the sentences as "worse than anything we imagined".
Last week, BIRD, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International were among 20 human rights groups which signed an open letter calling on Bahraini authorities to investigate what they described as "serious allegations of torture" in the case.
They said defendants had reported being "subjected to forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against themselves and their families, as well as citizenship revocation and deportation". Many were pressured to sign lengthy statements they were not allowed to read, they added.
The advocate general insisted on Monday that all the defendants' legal rights had been guaranteed during the investigation and that they had been given a fair trial.

Houthi fighters have advanced to within 100 km of Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, after government forces withdrew from positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Yemeni military sources said on Monday. Tankers carrying Saudi crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu to buyers in Asia pass through the strait .
Brent crude futures fell 2.32% to $93.62 a barrel at 9:43 a.m. ET, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) dropped 1.93% to 86.85. Murban, Abu Dhabi’s benchmark crude, rose 1.52% to 94.89.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters that Houthi fighters had reached Khor Omairh, about 100 km west of Aden. The government had said on Sunday it was pulling out of Dhubab and the surrounding area near the strait to defend the city. Maritime Executive reported on Nov. 3 that Houthi control of the coast between Bab el-Mandeb and Aden “would present a major increase in the threat posed to merchant shipping” using the strait and the Maritime Security Transit Corridor through the Gulf of Aden.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said on Thursday that the group struck Pumping Station No. 7 on the East-West Pipeline and the Yanbu oil facility, The New Arab reported . The group has vowed to keep attacking Saudi Arabia under a principle of “siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation,” Al Jazeera reported .
The Red Sea has been Saudi Arabia’s main oil export hub since the Iran war began in February, Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Monday. The East-West Pipeline can carry up to 7 million barrels per day from the kingdom’s eastern oilfields to Yanbu, according to The National . A drone attack in September that Riyadh blamed on a pro-Iranian militia in Iraq shut the line until Sept. 22.
Strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab told Al Jazeera that the Houthis aim their missile and drone campaign at Saudi Arabia, not at the authorities in Aden, and that the group’s gains along Bab el-Mandeb mean it “now directly and completely control[s] the western Yemeni coastal sector and part of the maritime extension towards Aden.”

articles.title_orig: 'iPhone 20 Pro' Rumored to Be Based on iPhone Air
articles.title_zh: 'iPhone 20 Pro' Rumored to Be Based on iPhone Air
articles.content_orig:
Next year's "iPhone 20 Pro" models will use the same glass design as the iPhone Air , but with more pronounced curvature along all four sides, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ."
In a new post on Weibo, the leaker said the device would use the same glass material as the ‌iPhone Air‌, adjusted to have greater curvature and produce a four-sided curved effect. The accompanying hashtag refers specifically to an "iPhone 20 Pro" with a four-sided curved, "all-glass" design.
An illustration shared with the post depicts rounded front and rear glass meeting a narrow, polished, gold-colored metallic frame. Physical side buttons, antenna lines, and a protruding rear camera assembly remain visible.
Taken together with earlier rumors and the post's accompanying illustration, the repeated comparisons suggest a design somewhere between the iPhone X and ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ provides a reference for the slim profile and a more modern iPhone design, while the more pronounced glass curvature recalls the rounded edges of the iPhone X. Both feature a polished frame.
The latest claim builds on Fixed Focus Digital's previous report that Apple had modified ‌iPhone Air‌ manufacturing equipment to produce more rounded glass components for the 20th anniversary models. The leaker said the changes had helped reduce manufacturing costs, while substantially improving thinness and heat dissipation.
In a still-earlier report , the same leaker also claimed that a supply chain facility had completed renovations ahead of "iPhone 20" production, with manufacturing quality expected to be roughly comparable to the first-generation ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back.
The broader design picture aligns with Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman 's reporting that Apple's anniversary Pro models will feature glass that curves into the sides from both the front and rear, with a thin metal band between the two panels. Gurman has also described thinner display bezels and curved glass around all corners and edges, in what he expects to be the biggest overhaul of the Pro line since the iPhone X.
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 . While leakers have variably referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," Apple's naming plans remain unclear. It seems plausible that the company could skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to its introduction of the iPhone X in 2017.

articles.title_orig: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.title_zh: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.title_zh: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.content_orig:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

articles.title_orig: Cantwell Accuses Commerce Department of Letting AI Chips Reach China as Xi Meeting Nears
articles.title_zh: Cantwell Accuses Commerce Department of Letting AI Chips Reach China as Xi Meeting Nears
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
articles.title_zh: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
articles.content_orig:
Sympathies have been expressed to a senior Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politician following the death of his wife and daughter within hours of each other.
The party said Lord Morrow, who is chairman of the DUP, lost his wife Lady Jennifer Morrow and their daughter Rachel Burrows at the weekend.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "words cannot adequately express the heartbreak and sorrow felt across our party".
"There are no words that can ease the pain of such an unimaginable loss," he added.
Lord Morrow is a former Stormont minister and a former assembly member for the Fermanagh and South Tyrone constituency.
A funeral notice for his daughter Rachel said she was a married mother of two children. It said she died on Sunday "peacefully surrounded by her loving family".
Robinson added that Lord Morrow's wife and daughter died "within hours of each other" on Sunday.
"On behalf of the Democratic Unionist Party, I extend our deepest sympathy to Maurice, to Rachel's husband John, and to the entire Morrow and Burrows families at this most difficult of times," he said.
"Maurice Morrow has been a rock of strength and support to so many of us through difficult moments in our lives. Now, in his darkest hour, it is our turn to be a rock for him.
"Throughout Jennifer and Rachel's long battles, Maurice has demonstrated extraordinary love and strength."
Speaking at Stormont, Robinson said the last couple of weeks for Lord Morrow would "have been incredibly difficult".
"But to lose your daughter and know how gravely ill your wife is, and to lose your wife some four hours later yesterday, is a deep personal shock and tragedy for him, for his surviving daughter Victoria, for Rachel's husband John and their two children, and for the wider Morrow and Burrows family."
Robinson said that as party chairman for the last 26 years, Lord Morrow has been "steadfast and fundamental to the foundations of the DUP".
"The commitment that runs through us runs through Maurice, and so this time all of us are here as colleagues to pay tribute to Maurice, to offer him comfort and prayers," he added.
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister also extended his sympathies to Lord Morrow and expressed "sincere Christian condolences".

articles.title_orig: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.title_zh: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on November 16, 2026
India’s push to expand domestic shipbuilding and lessen its dependence on China has found an eager partner in Korea, whose shipbuilders are looking for new production bases abroad.
Those complementary needs are driving a burgeoning partnership centered on Thoothukudi, a port city near India’s southern tip, where HD Hyundai plans to build a $4 billion shipyard with Indian state partners. On India’s west coast, Samsung Heavy Industries is backing an Indian yard competing for the country’s first oil tanker orders in decades.
The stakes reach beyond the two countries. China, Korea and Japan accounted for about 93 percent of global shipbuilding in 2024, according to Clarksons Research, and India is spending public money to become the fourth name on that list, with Korean partners instead of Chinese ones.
When India’s shipping minister visited Korea last month, he toured Korean shipyards and explored business opportunities with all three of Korea’s major shipbuilders, underscoring New Delhi’s push to expand its shipbuilding industry.
India’s Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal met HD Hyundai Chairman Chung Ki-sun, Samsung Heavy Industries CEO Choi Sung-an and Hanwha Ocean Executive Vice President Kim Chang-yong to ask for investment and technology transfer during a four-day trip that ended Oct. 28.
The tour was the latest in a series of attempts by New Delhi to import an industry it has not managed to build on its own. India ranks 12th in global shipbuilding and wants to be in the top five by 2047.
For Korean yards that are full at home and losing orders to China, it is a subsidized way to add capacity. The outcome will show whether a shipbuilding industry can be assembled outside East Asia from state funding and borrowed know-how.
About 95 percent of India’s trade by volume moves by sea, the country spends close to $75 billion a year hiring foreign ships, and its own yards held 0.5 percent of the global order book as of Sept. 1, according to the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO).
Indian cabinet earmarked 697.3 billion rupees ($7.4 billion) in September 2025 to lift annual capacity to 4.5 million gross tons by 2047. State-run buyers plan to order 437 vessels worth about 2.2 trillion rupees.
Demand is not the constraint but the ability to build is. Indian yards delivered about 65,000 deadweight tons of ships in the fiscal year through March 2025, roughly a fifth of a single supertanker. Cheap labor does not close the gap. An Indian yard needs 150 to 180 man-hours for work that takes 10 to 15 in Korea, Han Seung-han, an analyst at SK Securities, wrote in a September report.
“A policy of adding capacity does not by itself raise the ability to build ships,” Han wrote. “The capability to run a yard has to come in whole.”
Korean yards face the reverse problem. The industry is in a supercycle, and “domestic production capacity is almost full, with work backed up three to five years,” said Lee Kyu-seok, a senior research fellow at the Export-Import Bank of Korea’s Overseas Economic Research Institute. India, he added, appears to offer “a structure where it is easier to match production costs.”
Nor would Indian yards serve only India. “Shipbuilding is already globalized,” Lee said.
Among the partners India could have chosen, China, the largest builder, seems ruled out. “Because of the border dispute, India does not cooperate with China in strategic industries,” said Kim Kyung-hoon, head of the India and South Asia team at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
New Delhi has thawed ties with Beijing, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in September, but relations remain far from the level needed for industrial cooperation, he said. “Handing shipbuilding subsidies to China is unimaginable.”
Japan’s yards have moved on to specialized vessels, while India wants to start with container ships and large oil tankers, which Korean yards still build, Kim said. “Korea is almost the only partner.”
A similar rivalry looks to be pushing Korea toward India. Chinese yards won 63 percent of global new orders last year and Korean yards 21 percent, according to Clarksons Research. Korean builders now see Southeast Asia and India as partners that can help offset China, an industry representative familiar with the matter said.
“After Southeast Asia, India is the market drawing attention,” the representative said, adding that India is courting Korea’s three major shipbuilders to grow its own industry.
HD Hyundai is leading Korean shipbuilders’ foray into India. When Sonowal met Chung on Oct. 28, the two sides agreed to finish a detailed project report (DPR) on the yard’s cost, size and schedule within six months. The local port authority ordered a feasibility study in September, and site inspections are now underway.
HD Hyundai is to run the yard through a joint venture as its largest shareholder. Until it opens, India plans to place its first orders with HD Hyundai’s yards in Korea and send workers there for training. The partnership began with a Tamil Nadu state agreement in December 2025.
“The specific shareholding structure and investment size of the joint venture are under discussion with the relevant agencies and partners,” HD Hyundai said in a written response to the Korea JoongAng Daily. “However, under the [memorandum of understanding] signed among equity investors on the occasion of the Korea-India summit in April, our baseline is to secure at least 60 percent of the joint venture.”
What HD Hyundai gains is scale it cannot add at home. The yard is planned to turn out about 2.5 million gross tons a year, more than half of the capacity India wants nationwide by 2047. It would be the group’s third overseas base after Vietnam and the Philippines, and subsidies would carry much of the cost: Han estimates that central and state support will cover 45 to 47 percent of the $4 billion bill, leaving HD Hyundai to fund about $2.2 billion.
“We are looking to build a stable production system by securing both Indian domestic orders and global orders,” the company said. “Over the long term, we expect it to diversify our global production system by drawing on India’s abundant work force and growth potential, and to complement the production capacity of our domestic yards.”
Han expects the next round of global orders to center on tankers and bulk carriers, where competing with China comes down to cost. Nearly half of India’s 1,592 ships are more than 20 years old, and most are tankers or bulk carriers, he noted. “It cannot be solved with domestic yards,” Han wrote. “The answer is India, following Vietnam and the Philippines.”
Samsung Heavy Industries has taken a lighter route, lending know-how to an existing Indian yard instead of building one. It signed a cooperation deal in September 2025 with Swan Defence and Heavy Industries. Last month, Swan submitted the lowest bid for up to four product tankers for a venture led by the state-run Shipping Corporation of India, undercutting a Cochin Shipyard bid backed by HD Hyundai. The contract has not been finalized. Hanwha Ocean has so far held talks with state-run Hindustan Shipyard on ship design.
The agreements remain nonbinding, and investment terms and construction dates are still open.
The larger risk lies in India’s follow-through. The yard would take four to five years to build, Kim said, and until then New Delhi and Tamil Nadu have to keep paying subsidies, acquiring land and ordering ships through state firms. “Whether it keeps ordering ships as planned is the question mark,” Kim said. “How binding that cooperation becomes is the biggest question.”
The subsidies also have an end date. India’s shipbuilding aid is scheduled to run until March 2036, so a yard finished around 2031 would have about five years of assured support. “The 20 to 30 percent subsidies offset the cost gap,” Han wrote. “They do not resolve it structurally.”

articles.title_orig: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
articles.title_zh: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
articles.content_orig:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.
That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.
Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.
Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.
If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.
Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.
Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , text message or phone call claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.
"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.
New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.
There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.

In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.
Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.
"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.
"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."

articles.title_orig: Mexican president arrives in China for APEC summit, set to meet Xi
articles.title_zh: Mexican president arrives in China for APEC summit, set to meet Xi
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: The Lost Roman Legion That Vanished into Ancient China
articles.title_zh: The Lost Roman Legion That Vanished into Ancient China
articles.content_orig:
It is rumored that in 53 BC, thousands of Roman soldiers vanished after the Battle of Carrhae, and that the survivors settled in Han Dynasty China.
Published: Nov 16, 2026 written by Robert De Graaff , MA History
Published: Nov 16, 2026 written by Robert De Graaff , MA History
In 53 BC, ten thousand Roman legionaries vanished into the eastern deserts following the catastrophic Battle of Carrhae. Decades later, Chinese chroniclers recorded a mysterious foreign force fighting in a tight fish-scale formation thousands of miles away on the Silk Road. Did survivors of Rome’s worst defeat march across Asia to found a remote village in Han Dynasty China? What is the evidence to support this popular but unproven theory?
In 1957, American academic Homer Dubs published a paper theorizing the presence of a Roman legion in ancient China. The story begins in 53 BC when Marcus Licinius Crassus launched an invasion of Parthia to enhance his military reputation. He was killed, and his army was smashed at the Battle of Carrhae , where thousands were killed, and thousands more were taken prisoner.
The Parthians , not wanting to waste the manpower, found a use for the prisoners. The captured Romans were given back their weapons and equipment and pressed into service. It may seem strange to rely on an enemy for national security, but this practice was very common throughout history, especially in the ancient world. It is something the Parthians were known for.
Obviously, stationing these troops on the western border with Roman territory was out of the question. The legionaries were shipped off to the east to the far-flung reaches of the Parthian empire. They would end up in Central Asia, guarding against bandits and other threats in what is now Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Any direct mention of these soldiers ends there, but this is only the first part of the story.
Seventeen years later, the Romans may reappear in the historical record. Far to the east, Han China was expanding, spreading further and further west, setting up the Western Protectorate, areas under Chinese influence if not outright control. The Chinese clashed with Parthia at Zhizhi, modern-day Kazakhstan, and won a decisive victory. This secured Han China’s western flank, establishing Chinese presence in the region.
Chinese records of the battle mention something interesting. Some of the soldiers they fought against used what was described as a fish-scale pattern formation. Some scholars believe this is the famous Roman testudo formation, in which legionaries interlock their shields to protect against missile attacks, resembling the overlapping scales of a fish.
The Chinese were impressed by these soldiers, and once again, the Romans were employed by their captors. They were moved even further east, along the Chinese- Tibetan border, to guard against raids. Specifically, they were moved to a place called Liqian, which shares the name the Chinese gave Rome, roughly translated as “people of the West.”
Many inhabitants of Liqian today have Caucasian DNA and traditionally European features, such as lighter skin, lighter-colored eyes, and prominent noses. They are also generally much taller than their ethnic Chinese countrymen. So, is this proof that the Romans reached China and fought for the Han Dynasty?
While all of this evidence may seem compelling, the theory falls apart under closer scrutiny. The name Liqian was the Han Chinese name for Rome, but the same name was used for the Greek kingdoms in Central Asia founded by Alexander the Great and his successors . More than likely, with such limited contact between them, the name was more of a generic term for those of European descent, without any consideration for ethnic subdivisions. The fish scale formation does sound a lot like the testudo , but this is circumstantial. While it may be Romans whom the Chinese fought at Zhizhi, it may have been soldiers who copied Roman ways, or it may be something else altogether. A simple phrase is hardly conclusive evidence.
A significant portion of the Liqian locals indeed have Caucasian genes, but did it come from Romans, or the Greek kingdoms in Central Asia, whose people could have migrated along the well-established trade routes to Liqian? The nomadic peoples of the Eurasian Steppe, which runs from Hungary to Korea, are also a hodgepodge of ethnic groups, so having Caucasian genes from this source is not out of the question.
In truth, the absence of evidence is evidence of absence. To date, there have been no archaeological finds that support the idea of a Roman legion in central China along the Tibetan border. There have been no finds of Roman weapons, armor, or other military equipment , no coins, no religious votive offerings, or anything else associated with a significant Roman population.
Over the past few decades, Homer Dub’s theory linking the various pieces of evidence has generated much debate among scholars and history enthusiasts, but for now, the evidence is circumstantial. The idea of the presence of Romans in China belongs more to the realm of fiction than fact.
Robert is a history enthusiast who specializes in military history and dabbles in many other topics of the past. He is also a script writer for a popular history-focused YouTube channel.
